articles.title: You may be able to claim for Turner Brothers asbestos
articles.excerpt: Former workers, their families and people who lived near the Spotland factory can still claim, and there are routes for people exposed elsewhere too.
articles.content_html:
People made ill by asbestos from the former Turner Brothers Asbestos factory in Spotland can still claim compensation, 25 years after the company collapsed.

Former workers can claim, and so can people who never worked there, such as relatives exposed to dust on work clothes and people who lived near the factory.

Claims linked to Turner Brothers are handled by the T&N UK Asbestos Trust, which holds a separate fund for Turner Brothers claims. Its website is tandnasbestos.org.uk.

The trust usually pays a set share of a claim's full value rather than the whole amount.

People exposed to asbestos at other workplaces may also be able to claim, even if their employer closed long ago. Mesothelioma, a cancer caused by asbestos, often takes 40 to 50 years to show symptoms.

An employer's insurer is usually responsible even when the firm no longer exists. The Employers' Liability Tracing Office, at elto.org.uk, helps people find a former employer's insurer, though it does not pay compensation itself.

People diagnosed with mesothelioma who cannot trace a liable employer or insurer may be able to claim from the government's Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme, which pays according to age.

A government lump sum under the Pneumoconiosis etc. (Workers' Compensation) Act 1979 covers certain dust-related diseases when damages cannot be won from an employer, often because it has stopped trading. The claim form helpline is 0800 279 2322.

A separate 2008 mesothelioma scheme covers people exposed through a relative's work clothes, and people who cannot say where they were exposed but were exposed only in the UK.

Since 31 October 2026, dependants claiming under either government scheme after a sufferer died without claiming receive the full amount the sufferer would have been paid.

For a 60-year-old claimant under the 2008 scheme, that raises a dependant's payment from £24,526 to £56,656, according to the government. The change applies to new claims only.

Asbestos products were made at the Spodden Valley site from 1879 until 1998, and it was once the world's largest asbestos textile factory. Turner & Newall went into administration in 2001.

The site's owner, Spodden Park Ltd, began investigation works this month to map where asbestos is buried, ahead of a clean-up and redevelopment.

Compensation claims generally have to begin within three years of diagnosis, or within three years of a death. Some government payments must be claimed within 12 months.

The Greater Manchester Asbestos Victims Support Group, a registered charity, gives free advice on benefits and compensation to people with any asbestos-related disease, and runs support groups for patients and bereaved families.

The group can be contacted on 0161 258 0166, Monday to Friday from 9.30am to 4pm, or at info@gmavsg.org. Specialist asbestos solicitors can advise which routes apply, and many work on a no win, no fee basis.

Sources: T&N Asbestos Trustee Company, GOV.UK, Employers' Liability Tracing Office, Greater Manchester Asbestos Victims Support Group. Photograph: Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Rochdale deputy council leader detained twice in Pakistan
articles.excerpt: Rochdale deputy council leader Daalat Ali was detained twice within 10 days during a civic delegation visit to Pakistan.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale deputy council leader Daalat Ali was detained twice within 10 days during a civic delegation visit to Pakistan, the second time as he tried to fly home.

Ali was whisked into a side room by Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency after touching down in Islamabad on 19 October. He was questioned about his political background and held for around four hours without knowing what was happening.

After that first detention, Ali was taken to a meeting with the UK High Commissioner, who released him. He rejoined the Rochdale delegation in Sahiwal, where the visit aimed to build closer ties between Rochdale and Sahiwal.

Ali said officials did not know why they were holding him and that, when he asked whether he was under arrest, they said no. He said the authorities were professional throughout the process, though it was scary at first.

He was detained a second time on 28 October while attempting to return home from Lahore airport.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Rochdale councillor shares ‘scary’ detainment experience in Pakistan | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch Rochdale councillor shares ‘scary’ detainment experience in Pakistan George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter November 23, 2026 | 4:57 PM Print Councillor Daalat Ali's trip to Pakistan as part of a Rochdale council delegation to Sahiwal Daalat Ali feared he would never get home after being pulled off a flight back from Pakistan. Rochdale’s deputy council leader was detained twice in 10 days following a civic delegation in the country at the end of October. After touching down in Islamabad on October 19, he was whisked away into a side room by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), Pakistan’s primary federal law-enforcement, border control, and criminal investigation agency. They questioned him about his political background and kept there for around four hours without knowledge as to what was going on. They later took him to a meeting with the High Commissioner – the UK government’s representative – who let him go. The Kingsway ward representative said it was scary at first, but described the authorities as completely professional through the whole process. He joined back up with the Rochdale council delegation in Sahiwal – aimed at bringing closer ties between the two towns. “They didn’t know why they were holding me, “ Coun Ali added. “I went to the immigration desk and something came up on the computer. “We kept asking if I was under arrest and they said no. They didn’t seem to know why when we asked.” But when attempting to return home on October 28 from Lahore airport, the same thing happened again. This was when things really got scary for the Rochdalian. On both occasions, he wasn’t officially arrested, but a ‘notification on the computer’ when he was coming through airport security meant he was held for questioning once again. Coun Ali said: “Coming back, I was advised not to go to Kashmir. We were going to stay behind but I was asked not to go there because there is a lot going on there at the moment. “So I thought I would come back with the rest of the delegation and I changed my ticket and they stopped me again.” When asked how he felt after getting detained again, Coun Ali said: “I thought, this is how people go missing. I did worry I wasn’t going to come back when I was detained the second time. “I still don’t know why they stopped me. But on Monday (November 2) I was told by the High Commissioner’s office I could fly back so I booked my ticket and left.” Coun Ali ended up staying with a local politician he knew in the country during his extended stay, until he was able to fly home from Islamabad airport on November 4. Rochdale mayor, Coun Faisal Rana, stayed behind with him when he was held again – which Coun Ali ‘was extremely thankful’ for. Although Coun Ali never got answers as to why he was detained, he thinks it was as a result of his previous criticisms of the military administration currently operating in his birthplace of Kashmir. He added that his nephew in Islamabad was worried about hosting him out of fear he would face repercussions from the authorities. He believes the ordeal is connected to the extremely high political tensions in the Jammu and Kashmir regions of Pakistan at the moment. The Rochdale council delegation visit came months on from when activist group, the Jammu and Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee, led summer protests where dozens were killed after things got violent. Law enforcement and protestors were amongst the 40 reportedly killed in July. The JKJAAC were protesting the administration’s handling of the elections for seats in the local assembly, it is understood. The Pakistani government has since proscribed the JKJAAC as a terrorist group, something Amnesty International has described as a violation of freedom rights. In June, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for South Asia, Isabelle Lassee said: “Branding a grassroots organization as ‘terrorist’ on vague grounds, while simultaneously cutting the region off from the outside world, raises serious concerns regarding the Pakistani authorities’ conduct and their disregard for human rights. “The proscription of JKJAAC under anti-terror laws is disproportionate, unlawful and a violation of the right to freedom of association.” The Pakistani government also issued new restrictions on international media reporting in the country back on August 5. Pakistan is currently ranked 153th out of 180 on the World Press Freedom Index. According to Reporters Without Borders, Pakistan is one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists, with multiple murders each year that are often linked to cases of corruption or illegal trafficking and which go completely unpunished. Coun Ali described their regime as ‘oppressive’ and accused them of committing ‘acroticities’ in the area, which is concerning their relatives living in Rochdale and across the UK. “I don’t support oppression at all,” he explained. “I have seen martial law, but this is staunch martial law at its best. “I know of three families in Rochdale who have had relatives in Kashmir killed. If you speak out here in Rochdale they will abduct your relatives. They are undermining free speech. “If people here speak their relatives face consequences in Pakistan. It is not acceptable. “There is so much oppression there and it’s not covered in the media here because people are too scared to speak out. “In Kashmir it is like Gaza, medicine and food is being withheld. Nothing gets in or out.” Despite the issues he faced over in the country of his birth, Coun Ali described the actual Rochdale council delegation a success. Members of the group posted on social media with pictures and videos of their travels. The mayor was seen cutting the ribbon on a new eye hospital in the area as well as the Sewing Machine Centre by the Al-Mahmood Foundation, established by Humanity Care Relief. There were a number of visits during the trip, where Coun Ali spoke of after-care and health issues in the area. He shared his expertise as the portfolio holder for health and adult social care on Rochdale council and explained how he learned of the ‘amazing’ work being done by Deaf Reach in Sahiwal as well. “We went to Sahiwal and it was brilliant,” Coun Ali added. “The people were the best I have ever met and they were excellent and welcoming.” The trip, paid for by the councillors themselves, was understood to be aimed at strengthening relationships between Rochdale and Punjab city, Sahiwal. The two areas were ‘twinned’ in 1998, with many Rochdale residents having family roots in the city. The High Commission for Pakistan and the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office have both been approached for comment. articles.title: Rochdale White Ribbon vigil: where Wednesday's walk starts and how to join
articles.excerpt: Residents are invited to join a free White Ribbon Day vigil walk and service in Rochdale on Wednesday 25 November 2026, commemorating victims of violence and abuse.
articles.content_html:
Residents are invited to join a free White Ribbon Day vigil walk and service in Rochdale on Wednesday 25 November 2026, commemorating victims of violence and abuse.

The council says the walk begins at 5pm outside Number One Riverside on Smith Street, following introductory speeches. Participants will then walk through the town centre to St Mary in the Baum Parish Church on St Mary's Gate.

A service at the church is scheduled from 6pm until 7pm. The council says everyone is welcome and no booking is needed. Attendees are encouraged to bring LED tealights or candles.

The event is organised by Rochdale Borough Council and partners. The published programme names actor Cait Fitton, actor Callum Lill, activist Gemma Aitchison, White Ribbon ambassador Warren Betts and MP Elsie Blundell among the guest speakers. The council provides community.safety@rochdale.gov.uk for enquiries.

Anyone attending should check the council's listing for any last-minute changes to the arrangements.

articles.title: Middleton Library to explore ghost stories and the real history behind them
articles.excerpt: Middleton Library is hosting a free evening exploring local ghost stories and the historical records behind them on Thursday 26 November 2026.
articles.content_html:
Middleton Library is hosting a free evening exploring local ghost stories and the historical records behind them on Thursday 26 November 2026.

The Haunted Library runs from 4pm to 5.30pm at Middleton Library on Long Street, M24 6DU. The session is intended for adults and teenagers and combines local legends with investigation of photographs, newspaper reports and archival material.

Booking is required by noon on Thursday 26 November, the same day as the event. The council's event listing directs residents to Eventbrite for tickets. People planning to attend should check availability before travelling.

The event offers a chance to separate the stories that have circulated locally from the documented people and events that may have inspired them. The council lists middleton.library@rochdale.gov.uk as the contact for enquiries.

articles.title: Thinking about fostering? Free advice stall at Rochdale Riverside on Wednesday
articles.excerpt: People considering becoming foster carers can speak to Rochdale Borough Council's fostering team at a free information stall on Wednesday 25 November 2026.
articles.content_html:
People considering becoming foster carers can speak to Rochdale Borough Council's fostering team at a free information stall on Wednesday 25 November 2026.

The drop-in takes place at Rochdale Riverside on Riverside Walk, OL16 1TR, from noon until 2pm. No appointment or booking is required, and the council says the session is open to everyone.

The regular monthly stall is intended for people who want to ask questions before deciding whether to pursue fostering. Visitors can discuss the process directly with council staff rather than committing to an application.

The council lists Fostering@rochdale.gov.uk as the contact address. Residents should consult the official event listing if they need to check the arrangements before travelling.

articles.title: Overwhelming support for veterans' flats plan at Denehurst House
articles.excerpt: Plans for five flats for veterans at Denehurst House have moved closer after a council consultation showed overwhelming support, with Rochdale Council's Cabinet due to decide.
articles.content_html:
Plans to create homes for veterans at Denehurst House have moved a step closer after Rochdale Council said a public consultation showed "overwhelming support" for the proposals.

The historic property is being upgraded to include a public café and five flats for veterans. Concerns about its ownership and legal status prompted the council, which is the legal trustee of Denehurst House and Park, to launch a review and consultation.

A report to the council's Cabinet, which is due to consider the matter tomorrow, says no objections had been received from the public up to the date of the report.

It states: "The consultation showed overwhelming support for use of the property for veterans' accommodation in perpetuity."

If Cabinet approves the proposal, the five flats will be designated as residential accommodation for veterans. The source does not give a timetable for the works beyond the Cabinet decision.

articles.title: Redwood School praised by Ofsted for preparing learners for next steps
articles.excerpt: Ofsted has praised Redwood School in Rochdale, a maintained school for children and young people with SEND, after a September inspection.
articles.content_html:
Ofsted has praised Redwood School, a Rochdale school for children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), saying its learners are superbly prepared for their next steps.

Inspectors visited Redwood School in September and inspected it under Ofsted's new inspection framework. They found strong standards in five of seven areas, and the school met expected standards in achievement and in curriculum and teaching.

The report says leaders place inclusion at the cornerstone of the school's work. It also says Redwood staff turn Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) goals into meaningful and precise targets, drawing on detailed assessments, specialist advice and clear family communication.

An EHCP is a legal document for young people with SEND up to the age of 25. It outlines their educational, health and social care needs and the provision required to meet them.

Redwood School is maintained by Rochdale Borough Council, which published the news on its website. The school's next steps in the inspection process are not set out in the source material.

Published: 23 November 2026 A Rochdale school that teaches children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) has been praised by Ofsted. Oftsed praised the school for creating an environment where ‘there is no ceiling on what pupils can achieve’. This was highlighted in a glowing inspection of Redwood School by the education regulator who also praised how leaders ‘place inclusion at the cornerstone of the school’s work’ and how ‘pupils at all stages are ready and confident to learn’. Inspectors visited the special school, maintained by Rochdale Borough Council, in September and under the new inspection framework, they found strong standards in 5 out of 7 areas. These areas were inclusion, attendance and behaviour, leadership and governance, personal development and wellbeing, and post-16 provision. The school also met expected standards in its achievement and curriculum and teaching. Within the report, Redwood is recognised for drawing on detailed assessments, specialist advice and clear communication with families to ‘skilfully turn’ pupils' education, health and care plan (EHCP) goals into meaningful and precise targets. EHCPs are a legal document given to children and young people up to the age of 25 with SEND which outlines their educational, health and social care needs and the provision that must be implemented in order to help them achieve key life outcomes. Ofsted also highlighted how the school’s careful adaptations to meet a diverse and complex range of needs enable pupils to make ‘meaningful progress from their individual starting points’. Specific praise was also given to Redwood's sixth form provision, which operates across 3 campuses in Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton and supports learners aged 16 to 19. Described as a significant strength of the school, Ofsted commented on how pupils are ‘superbly prepared for their next steps’ and that its unwavering focus on developing independence and preparing pupils well for their future lives, ran as ‘a golden thread through every aspect of school life’. The school’s post-16 curriculum was further labelled as ‘ambitious’ and ‘aspirational’ and noted for having ‘a clear focus on removing barriers and maximising what every student can achieve’. Learners increasingly develop the confidence, independence and skills that they need as a result. Reflecting on the school’s recent inspection, Paul Evans, headteacher of Redwood School, said: “We are extremely pleased with the outcome and would like to thank our entire school community for their continued support. “The report reflects the hard work, dedication and commitment of our staff, learners, families and governors, and we are incredibly proud of what has been achieved together. “We would like to extend a heartfelt thank you to all parents and carers for your ongoing encouragement, partnership and support. Your contribution plays a vital role in helping our learners thrive and achieve their best.” Redwood School was last inspected in June 2022 when it was rated ‘Good’. Spread across 6 sites in total, Redwood supports more than 350 pupils with a range of learning difficulties, social, emotional and mental health needs, autism spectrum disorder and multi-sensory impairment. Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, added: “This report is a fantastic endorsement of the outstanding work taking place across Redwood School. "The school's commitment to inclusion, ambition and supporting every child to reach their full potential shines through in Ofsted's findings, including on its efforts to prepare young people for independent and fulfilling lives beyond school. articles.title: Girls waiting for CAMHS support get free football programme
articles.excerpt: A 36-week free football programme for girls aged six to 11 waiting for or receiving Rochdale CAMHS support has begun, run by Pennine Care and Rochdale AFC Community Trust.
articles.content_html:
Girls aged six to 11 who are waiting for or receiving support from Rochdale's child and adolescent mental health service can now take part in a free football programme.

Pennine Care NHS and Pennine Care Charity have teamed up with Rochdale AFC Community Trust on the 36-week pilot, which aims to build girls' confidence, social skills and emotional wellbeing.

The programme was developed after feedback from parents of children receiving CAMHS support. Parents said their children needed activities to build self-esteem and make friends.

Sessions are delivered by experienced staff from Rochdale AFC Community Trust. So far 16 girls have taken part, and early feedback indicates they are enjoying the sessions and building confidence and friendships.

Anders Cox, clinical lead at Heywood, Middleton and Rochdale CAMHS, said the sessions were designed around what families had asked for.

The service is run by Pennine Care NHS Foundation Trust, which said the pilot would be free to participants.

What changes for families in Rochdale

  • The 36-week pilot is free to girls aged six to 11 waiting for or receiving Rochdale CAMHS support.
  • Sixteen girls have taken part so far, with sessions delivered by Rochdale AFC Community Trust staff.

articles.title: Police invite parents to station over youth group's behaviour
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police plan to invite the parents of a group of youths to a police station after reports of criminal damage, theft and assaults.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester Police have asked parents to speak to their children about the behaviour of a group of youths in Heywood, and plan to invite the parents to a police station.

The force said the group has caused criminal damage, theft and assaults, and has been behaving in a generally intimidating way. The request was posted by GMP on Facebook.

Police said they identified the children through personal interactions and by reviewing CCTV footage obtained via schools and partner agencies. They said they will shortly invite parents and youths into the police station.

GMP said Criminal Behaviour Orders may be put in place for the youths if the behaviour continues, but added that it would like to avoid reaching that stage for the children involved.

Rochdale Daily has asked Greater Manchester Police for comment.

articles.title: Castleton house approved for eight-bed care home
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has approved plans to turn a house on Thornham New Road, Castleton, into a care home for up to eight adults.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has approved plans to turn a house at 9 Thornham New Road, Castleton, into a care home for up to eight adults, with 24-hour care.

The council approved the application on 18 November. The plans include a new upstairs bay window and internal layout changes to the property.

The council received 20 comments on the application. Residents raised concerns about parking, noise and emergency vehicle access to the home.

Highways officers did not object to the application and said the home was unlikely to add much traffic. The driveway has room for three or four cars, and the council requires two parking spaces for a care home of this size.

The applicant says no more than two staff would be on site at once. A planning condition limits the care home to eight residents and requires work to start within three years of approval.

What it means for Castleton

  • The care home is limited to eight residents and must start work within three years of approval.
  • The council requires two parking spaces for a care home of this size, and the driveway has room for three or four cars.

events.content_html:
Queen's Park Café in Heywood is hosting Breakfast with Santa on six mornings between Saturday 12 and Wednesday 23 December, each running from 10.30am to 12pm.

The dates are Saturday 12, Sunday 13, Saturday 19, Sunday 20, Monday 21 and Wednesday 23 December.

Children's tickets cost £16 and include a children's breakfast and a drink, Christmas craft and colouring, a Christmas present for each child, and a meet and greet with Santa. Adult tickets cost £10 for a traditional English breakfast with instant coffee or tea.

Bookings can be made by messaging the café on Facebook, calling in at the café, or messaging 07983 737871. Spaces are only secured once paid in full and booked in advance, and the café asks families to mention any allergies when booking.
